title: The Influence of Light Colour Temperatures on Interior Design Student Performance in Classroom Studies
research_question: How do lighting conditions (daylight, high, and low colour temperatures) impact interior design students' perceived spatial quality, comfort, collaboration, motivation, distraction, and fatigue in a classroom studio?

participants.description: Interior design students (39.5% male, 60.5% female; 86.3% aged 18-24 years, 13.7% aged 25-34 years) from Irbid University College, Jordan. Most were first-year (65.3%) and attended design studios 1-2 times per week (59.7%).
participants.recruitment: Students studying interior design at Irbid University College were selected as the target population for the study.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: A design studio (80 m²) at Irbid University College, Jordan, with manipulated light colour temperatures: Daylight, High Colour Temperature, and Low Colour Temperature conditions. A 'High Light scenario' was presented (Figure 1a), and the studio's 'current conditions' were also shown (Figure 1b).

mechanisms: High colour temperatures, including daylight, mimic natural lighting environments, offering higher contrast and brightness, which enhances spatial quality, focus, attentiveness, and reduces fatigue.

Warm white and other low-light colour temperatures may produce a comfortable and personal ambience, encouraging cooperation and interpersonal communication (though this is contradicted by some findings).
moderators: Nature of the task carried out in the design studio
implementation_implications: Educational spaces should be designed with lighting systems that provide abundant natural light, high colour temperatures, and appropriate brightness levels to create comfortable and efficient learning atmospheres.
Lighting conditions should be improved to increase the sense of space, support and motivate learners' learning habits, and make the learning setting more pleasant and appealing.
Consider diverse preferences of students and regularly seek feedback to ensure lighting meets their needs and preferences.

Pearson Correlation Analysis between Individual Productivity, Spatial Quality, Social Adaptation, and Daylight, High, and Low colour temperatures.

limitations: Sample size was limited to 124 interior design students from a specific university, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to a larger population.
The study relied on self-reported data, which could be subject to biases or inaccuracies.
The study focused only on the impact of light colour temperatures and did not consider other potential factors that could influence students' experiences in design studios.
